scenes.narration: In this video, we're going to talk about blood pressure and its two numbers. By the end, you'll know what blood pressure measures, what systolic and diastolic mean, when a reading counts as high, and how to keep it healthy.

scenes.narration: Most people with high blood pressure feel perfectly well, with no warning signs at all. Yet inside, the pressure can stay high for years. The World Health Organization estimates that 46 percent of them don't know it. So how would you know?

scenes.narration: So what is blood pressure? It is the force of blood pushing against the walls of your arteries. Let's look inside one. With every heartbeat, blood surges in and presses outward on the wall. The elastic wall stretches, then springs back. We measure this pressure in millimetres of mercury.

scenes.narration: Now watch one heartbeat. The heart contracts, and a pressure wave travels along the artery. The pressure peaks: this is the systolic pressure. Then the heart rests, and the pressure falls to its lowest: the diastolic pressure. Together, these two values make your reading.

scenes.narration: To measure it, an inflatable cuff goes around the upper arm. It squeezes the arm, and a monitor shows two numbers. The top number is the systolic pressure, here 120. The bottom number is the diastolic, here 80. We say this reading is 120 over 80.

scenes.narration: For most adults, 90 over 60 or lower is low. The ideal range is between 90 over 60 and 120 over 80. Between 120 over 80 and 140 over 90, you're at risk. And 140 over 90 or higher is high blood pressure, called hypertension. It is diagnosed when readings are that high on two different days.

scenes.narration: Year after year, high pressure strains the arteries and damages their walls. In the heart, that can mean a heart attack. In the brain, a stroke. In the kidneys, kidney damage. And a heart forced to pump harder can eventually fail: that is heart failure.

scenes.narration: The good news: you can keep it healthy. Eat less than 5 grams of salt a day, just under a teaspoon. Eat more vegetables and fruit. Be physically active. Avoid tobacco, and limit alcohol. And have your blood pressure checked regularly.

scenes.narration: The most common mistake is thinking: I feel fine, so my blood pressure must be normal. But most people with it feel nothing at all. Only a measurement can tell. So measure it, and remember: a diagnosis needs high readings on two different days.
